newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala sees 30 million 100-lb bag sugar harvest.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala sees 30 million 100-lb bag sugar harvest.

text.p: Guatemala will produce 30 million 100-lb bags of sugar during the 1996-1997 harvest, up from 28.2 million in the last harvest, Sugar Growers Association of Guatemala said Wednesday.

Armando Boesche, manager of the association, told Reuters that predictions for a larger harvest were based on an additional 5,000 to 8,000 hectares of sugar in production this year, as well as hopes for better yields.
Boesche said 15 of the country's 17 sugar mills are in production and he expects all to be up and running soon and throughout most of the harvest, which lasts through June.
Sugar growers anticipate they will export approximately 70 percent of the crop, in keeping with previous harvests, said Boesche.

Boesche said heavy rains over the past weekend may have caused a few days of backup in some mills but "in comparison with the last harvest at this time last year we have produced a greater quantity of sugar."

He said so far this year, yields of cane per hectare were a little better than last harvest's 93 tonnes per hectare. The yield of sugar per tonne of cane was approximately 10.3 percent this year at the high end of last year's range.
Guatemala has no direct contracts to sell sugar to other countries and sells all of its exports FOB through the NYCSC exchange, said Boesche.

The principal traders who bought Guatemala sugar in the last harvest were Louis Dreyfus, Czarnikow, E.D. & F. Man and Commodity Specialist. Principal destinations of Guatemalan sugar were the United States, Peru, Russia and Venezuela.
Boesche said 11 percent of Guatemala's last harvest was absorbed by sales to the United States under the quota system.
But, due to an increase this year in Mexico's cuota, Guatemala's portion has dropped this year, said Boesche.
Guatemalan sugar will represent 4.58 percent of U.S. imports instead of 4.87 percent in the last harvest.
Boesche said Guatemala had no strategy for counterracting the lower quota. "What can we do?" said Boesche.
Boesche said Guatemala sells most of its sugar before the start of a new harvest and has "no significant stocks" at this time.

Most of Guatemala's mills are older, and no new ones have opened in the last ten years, though two have closed since 1985. Boesche said there is no significant international investment in the Guatemalan sugar industry.
